two-sum.pattern: Hash map of value → index (look up the complement)

approaches.name: Try every pair
approaches.idea: Check every pair of different positions and return the one whose values add up to `target`.
steps: For each `i`, and each `j > i`:
If `nums[i] + nums[j] == target`, return `[i, j]`.
approaches.why: n(n − 1)/2 pairs, each checked in O(1). In C++ the sum is computed in `long long`, since two values near 10⁹ overflow an `int`.

approaches.name: Sort the indices, then two pointers
approaches.idea: Sorting lets two pointers find the pair in one pass, but the answer needs the original indices — so sort the indices by their values instead of the values themselves.
steps: Make an array of indices `0..n − 1` and sort it by `nums[index]`.
Put `i` at the first and `j` at the last sorted position.
If the two values sum to `target`, return their original indices; if the sum is too small move `i` right, otherwise move `j` left.
approaches.why: Sorting dominates at O(n log n); the two-pointer scan is O(n). The index array takes O(n) memory.

approaches.name: One pass with a hash map
approaches.idea: For each value, the partner it needs is `target − nums[i]`. Remember every value seen so far with its index; if the partner was already seen, the pair is found.
steps: Create an empty map from value to index.
For each `i`, compute `need = target − nums[i]`.
If `need` is in the map, return `[map[need], i]`.
Otherwise store `nums[i] → i` and continue.
approaches.why: One pass with O(1) average map operations. Checking before inserting means an element is never paired with itself, while two equal values at different indices still match.

contains-duplicate.pattern: Hash set membership (have I seen this before?)

approaches.name: Compare every pair
approaches.idea: A duplicate exists if some pair of positions holds the same value.
steps: For each `i` and each `j > i`, if `nums[i] == nums[j]`, return true.
If no pair matches, return false.
approaches.why: n(n − 1)/2 comparisons. For n = 10⁵ that is about 5 × 10⁹ — far too slow.

approaches.name: Sort, then compare neighbours
approaches.idea: After sorting, equal values sit next to each other, so one pass over neighbours finds any duplicate.
steps: Sort `nums`.
For each `i` from 1, if `nums[i] == nums[i − 1]`, return true.
Return false.
approaches.why: The sort dominates. It needs no extra structure beyond the sort's own stack, but it changes the input order.

approaches.name: Hash set of values seen so far
approaches.idea: Walk the array once, remembering each value in a set. Meeting a value that is already in the set means it appears twice.
steps: Create an empty set.
For each value: if it is in the set, return true; otherwise add it.
Return false after the loop.
approaches.why: One pass with O(1) average set operations; the set may hold all n values when they are distinct.

valid-anagram.pattern: Frequency counting (array of 26 counts as a hash map)

approaches.name: Cross off each letter of s in t
approaches.idea: For every letter of `s`, find an unused copy of it in `t` and cross it off. If some letter has no copy left, or the lengths differ, they are not anagrams.
steps: If the lengths differ, return false.
Keep a `used` flag for each position of `t`.
For each letter of `s`, scan `t` for an unused position with the same letter; if none, return false; otherwise mark it used.
Return true.
approaches.why: Each of the n letters may scan all n positions of `t`. The flags take O(n).

approaches.name: Sort both strings and compare
approaches.idea: Anagrams become the same string once their letters are sorted.
steps: If the lengths differ, return false.
Sort the letters of both strings.
Return whether the sorted strings are equal.
approaches.why: Two sorts of n letters; the sorted copies take O(n) memory.

approaches.name: Count letters up for s and down for t
approaches.idea: Keep one count per letter: add 1 for each letter of `s` and subtract 1 for each letter of `t`. They are anagrams exactly when every count ends at 0.
steps: If the lengths differ, return false.
For each index `i`, increase `count[s[i]]` and decrease `count[t[i]]`.
Return true if all 26 counts are 0.
approaches.why: One pass over both strings; the table has a fixed 26 entries. (For Unicode input, use a hash map instead — still O(n).)

first-unique-character-in-a-string.pattern: Two passes with a frequency table (count first, then scan in order)

approaches.name: For each character, check the whole string
approaches.idea: A character is unique if no other position holds the same character. Check each position in order and return the first unique one.
steps: For each index `i`, scan all `j != i`.
If no `s[j] == s[i]`, return `i`.
Return −1 if every character repeats.
approaches.why: Each of the n positions may compare against all n others.

approaches.name: Count every letter, then find the first with count 1
approaches.idea: First count how often each letter appears. Then walk the string from the start; the first letter whose count is 1 is the answer.
steps: Count each letter of `s` in a 26-entry table.
Scan `s` from index 0; return the first `i` with `count[s[i]] == 1`.
Return −1 if none.
approaches.why: Two linear passes; the table has a fixed 26 entries.

group-anagrams.pattern: Hash map from a canonical key (sorted letters or letter counts) to its group

approaches.name: Compare each word with the first word of every group
approaches.idea: Keep a list of groups. For each word, check it against one member of every existing group with an anagram test; join the group that matches, or start a new one.
steps: Start with no groups.
For each word, walk through the groups and test whether it is an anagram of the group's first word (compare letter counts).
Add the word to the first matching group, or create a new group for it.
Return the groups.
approaches.why: A word may be compared with up to n groups, each comparison O(L) for words of length up to L. The output holds every word.

approaches.name: Group by the sorted word
approaches.idea: All anagrams have the same letters in sorted order, so the sorted word is a key that identifies the group. A hash map from key to list does the grouping in one pass.
steps: Create a map from key to list of words.
For each word, sort its letters to get the key and append the word to that key's list.
Return the map's lists.
approaches.why: Each of the n words is sorted in O(L log L). The map stores every word once plus its key.

approaches.name: Group by letter counts
approaches.idea: Counting the 26 letters of a word gives a key without sorting. Anagrams have identical counts, so they share a key.
steps: For each word, count its letters into 26 slots.
Turn the counts into a key (for example the counts joined by `#`).
Append the word to the map entry for that key.
Return the map's lists.
approaches.why: Each word is counted in O(L) and its key built in O(26). The map stores every word.

longest-consecutive-sequence.pattern: Hash set, extending runs only from their first value

approaches.name: From every value, count upwards with a linear search
approaches.idea: From each value `x`, look for `x + 1`, `x + 2`, … by scanning the array each time, and count how far the run goes.
steps: For each value `x`, set `len = 1`.
While the array contains `x + len` (found by scanning the whole array), increase `len`.
Keep the largest `len`; return it (0 for an empty array).
approaches.why: n starting values, each run up to n long, and each step a linear scan of n values.

approaches.name: Sort, then count runs
approaches.idea: After sorting, consecutive values sit next to each other. Walk the sorted array counting the current run, ignoring duplicates.
steps: If the array is empty, return 0. Sort it.
Walk from index 1: if the value equals the previous one, skip it (a duplicate); if it is previous + 1, extend the run; otherwise start a new run of length 1.
Keep the longest run and return it.
approaches.why: The sort dominates; the scan is O(n). The problem asks for O(n), which this misses.

approaches.name: Hash set; only start counting at the beginning of a run
approaches.idea: Put every value in a set. A value `x` starts a run only if `x − 1` is not in the set; only from those starts count `x + 1, x + 2, …` with O(1) lookups.
steps: Add every value to a set.
For each value `x` in the set: if `x − 1` is in the set, skip it (it is not a run start).
Otherwise count upwards while `x + len` is in the set.
Keep the longest run and return it.
approaches.why: Each value is the inside of a counted run at most once, because counting starts only at run starts — so all the counting loops together take O(n). The set holds up to n values.

valid-sudoku.pattern: Hash sets per row, column and box (seen-before checks)

approaches.name: Check rows, then columns, then boxes
approaches.idea: Check each of the 27 units (9 rows, 9 columns, 9 boxes) on its own with a fresh "seen" table; a digit seen twice in a unit makes the board invalid.
steps: For each row, scan its 9 cells with a fresh set; a repeated digit means invalid.
Do the same for each column.
Do the same for each 3 × 3 box, whose cells are `(3·(b / 3) + k / 3, 3·(b % 3) + k % 3)` for `k = 0..8`.
If no unit repeats a digit, return true.
approaches.why: For an n × n board each cell is read three times (once per unit type). With n = 9 this is a fixed 243 reads, so constant in practice; each set holds at most n digits.

approaches.name: One pass with a seen table for every unit
approaches.idea: Visit each cell once and check its digit against three tables at the same time: its row, its column and its box (box index `(r / 3)·3 + c / 3`).
steps: Keep `rows[9][10]`, `cols[9][10]` and `boxes[9][10]` flags (or bitmasks).
For each filled cell `(r, c)` with digit `d`, compute `b = (r / 3)·3 + c / 3`.
If `d` is already marked in `rows[r]`, `cols[c]` or `boxes[b]`, return false; otherwise mark it in all three.
Return true after all cells.
approaches.why: Each of the n² cells is read once with O(1) checks. The three tables have n × n flags; for n = 9 both are constant.

first-missing-positive.pattern: Index as a hash key (cyclic placement: value v belongs at index v − 1)

approaches.name: Try 1, 2, 3, … and scan for each
approaches.idea: The answer is the first positive integer not in the array. Test 1, then 2, and so on, scanning the whole array for each.
steps: Scan the array for `k`; if it is not there, return `k`.
This stops by `k = n + 1` at the latest, because n values cannot cover n + 1 numbers.
approaches.why: Up to n + 1 candidates, each needing a full O(n) scan.

approaches.name: Hash set of the values
approaches.idea: Put every value in a set; then check 1, 2, 3, … with O(1) lookups.
steps: Add all values to a set.
For `k` from 1 to n + 1, return the first `k` not in the set.
approaches.why: Building the set and checking up to n + 1 candidates are both O(n), but the set breaks the O(1) extra space requirement.

approaches.name: Cyclic placement: put each value v at index v − 1
approaches.idea: Only the values 1..n can matter (the answer is at most n + 1). Use the array itself as the set: swap each such value into its home slot `v − 1`. Afterwards the first slot `i` that does not hold `i + 1` gives the answer.
steps: For each index `i`: while `1 <= nums[i] <= n` and `nums[nums[i] − 1] != nums[i]`, swap `nums[i]` into its home slot `nums[i] − 1`.
Scan `i` from 0: the first `i` with `nums[i] != i + 1` means `i + 1` is missing — return it.
If every slot is correct, return `n + 1`.
approaches.why: Every swap puts one value into its home slot for good, so there are at most n swaps in total across all the while loops. The check `nums[nums[i] − 1] != nums[i]` stops endless swapping on duplicates. Only the input array is used.
